sections.title: Author Biography, Foreword, and Preface
sections.summary: This section gives Rashad Khalifa's biography as a Sufi-raised Egyptian who studied plant biochemistry in the United States and worked at Anheuser-Busch, along with his record of Muslim community service. Sulayman Shahid Mufassir's introduction frames the book's findings as faith-strengthening evidence comparable to the reassurance God gave the prophet Abraham. Khalifa's own preface describes how translating the Qur'an into English in 1968 stalled at the mysterious letters Alif Lam Mim opening sura Al-Baqara, prompting four years of research that culminated in a computerized letter count of the whole Qur'an. A table of contents lists the book's chapter structure.

sections.title: Prologue: The Qur'an's Perpetual Miracle
sections.summary: The prologue argues that the Qur'an itself is Muhammad's miracle, citing verses that challenge humans and jinn to produce anything comparable. It lists examples the author considers scientific miracles already stated in the Qur'an, including the earth's rotation, the sun as a light source versus the moon's reflected light, and the preservation of the Pharaoh's body. It argues the Qur'an contains no statements ever disproven by science, contrasts this with the era's widespread superstitions, and notes God's vow to preserve the Qur'an, concluding that the mysterious Qur'anic Initials letters are another facet of this perpetual, ongoing miracle.

sections.title: Compilation and Preservation of the Qur'an Text
sections.summary: These pages narrate the traditional account of how the Qur'an was recorded and preserved unaltered, describing the Prophet Muhammad's personal supervision of the writing of revelation through his scribe Zeid ibn Thabit. It recounts how, after martyrs at the Battle of Yamama died with the Qur'an memorized, Umar ibn Al-Khattab urged Caliph Abu Bakr to have Zeid collect the Qur'an into a single written volume, which later passed to Hafsa, and how Caliph Uthman had Zeid and three others reproduce standardized copies sent to Basra, Kufa, Damascus, and Mecca after Huzeifa ibn Al-Yaman reported recitation variations among Muslims in Syria and Iraq. The author argues these copies are the source of all Qur'ans published today.

sections.title: The Qur'anic Initials Defined
sections.summary: Chapter 2 defines the Qur'anic Initials as the sets of Arabic letters prefixing 28 of the Qur'an's 114 suras (one sura has two sets), formed from 14 distinct letters out of the 28-letter alphabet, which Sufi mystics traditionally call the illumination letters. It lists the 14 letters involved and presents tables of the 14 different initial sets and which suras contain them, in both recorded order (Table 5) and chronological revelation order (Table 6).

sections.title: Review of the Literature on the Qur'anic Initials
sections.summary: Chapter 3 surveys prior scholarly theories about the Qur'anic initials drawn from Al-Suyuti and Al-Baydawi, noting unanimous agreement among Muslim scholars that the letters relate to the Qur'an's miraculous nature. It lists predominant theories, including that the letters are a literary challenge, an attention-getting device, secret names of God or of the Qur'an, or foreign words, and recounts Ibn Abbas's view that Alif Lam Mim spells out God, Gabriel, and Muhammad. The bulk of the section reproduces Abdullah Yusuf Ali's detailed appendix analyzing patterns in how the abbreviated letters occur and offering tentative, admittedly speculative, symbolic interpretations for specific letter combinations across many suras.

sections.title: Development of the Research and Methods of Calculation
sections.summary: Chapter 4 describes hypotheses the author tested and discarded, such as correlating the initials with God's names or with prophets' names occurring in the same sura, before deciding to physically count every letter in all 114 suras with electronic computers. Chapter 5 details the manual tally method using a hand-marked form, then the FORTRAN IV programming on a Xerox Data Systems Sigma 7 computer that calculated each letter's absolute frequency, its percentage of a sura's total letters, and its average occurrence per verse, using sura Al-Baqara's letters Alif, Lam, and Mim as a worked example. It also explains the statistical caution required when comparing very short suras.

sections.title: The Letter Qaf in Sura Qaf and Sura Al-Shura
sections.summary: This section argues that sura Qaf, titled after and initialed with the letter Qaf, contains the highest frequency of that letter of any sura except three very short suras, which it shows are numerically inferior once absolute frequency and average-per-verse values are considered. It further observes that sura Qaf and the only other Qaf-initialed sura, Al-Shura, each contain exactly 57 occurrences of the letter Qaf, whose sum (114) equals the total number of suras in the Qur'an, offered as evidence that no human author, and only God, could have controlled such a distribution across a revelation spanning 23 years.

sections.title: The Letter Nun in Sura Al-Qalam
sections.summary: This section examines the initial Nun in sura Al-Qalam (The Pen), showing it ranks near the top in percentage frequency of Nun among all suras once its three highest competitors are re-averaged with their own initialed sister suras (Al-Shu'ara, Al-Dukhan, Al-Hijr). After this averaging, only Al-Saffat and Al-Waqi'a retain a higher percentage, but both fall below sura Al-Qalam in average per-verse frequency, leading the author to conclude that no sura has all three frequency measures of Nun higher than Al-Qalam.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.summary: Chapter 7 summarizes the mathematical properties found for each of the 14 Qur'anic initials in a master table, then draws several broader conclusions: that the Qur'an's letter-level composition proves it is God's word, illustrated by a calculated figure of 11 raised to the 414th power (roughly 6.26 x 10^26) possible letter arrangements; that the recorded and revelation orders of suras are each divinely confirmed by different initial groups; that the Meccan or Medinan locations of revelation are confirmed; that the Qur'an's distinctive spelling conventions must never be modernized; that verse divisions must never be altered, criticizing Yusuf Ali's rearrangement of a verse boundary in sura Ali-Imran; and that Bismillah is an integral verse of every sura except Al-Tawba. It closes by noting the number 14 recurs suggestively across 14 centuries and 14 letters, and offers a simplified thought experiment about the impossibility of a human controlling multi-letter distributions across a book's chapters.

sections.title: Addendum: Gematria of the Qur'anic Initials
sections.summary: The addendum recounts a hadith in which Jewish scripturists calculated the abjad numerical value of Alif Lam Mim as 71 and challenged Islam's longevity on that basis, to which the Prophet is reported to have replied by citing other initialed combinations (ALMS, ALR, ALMR). The author then applies the same ancient gematria system to all 14 sets of Qur'anic initials, weighting each by its frequency of occurrence, and presents a table arriving at a grand total the text suggests may indicate the lifespan of Islam, while noting this is offered only as a further illustration of the initials' multidimensional nature.
